newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian rights group condemns child "slavery".
newsitem.headline: Nigerian rights group condemns child "slavery".

text.p: A leading Nigerian human rights group condemned on Thursday what it called a frightening surge in the sale of children into bonded labour, prostitution and domestic slavery.
"The kidnap and sale or attempted sale of children in Nigeria has...in the last two to three years, assumed frightening proportions," the Constitutional Rights Project said in a report.

Harrowing tales were told of children who had been abducted or even sold by their parents, to be smuggled into neighbouring countries, forced into prostitution or made to work unpaid as domestic servants.
The blame for the upsurge in child dealing was laid squarely at the door of poverty.

Already mired in economic recession due to a long-term fall in oil prices, Africa's most populous nation slumped further into poverty after 1993 when a wave of strikes and violent protests followed the annulment of presidential elections by a former military government.

"Middlemen go out scouting for families with more children than they can cater for. They convince such families of the juicy employment opportunities awaiting their wards in the city, inside Nigeria and outside Nigeria," the report said.
Ten-year-old Chukwudi Joseph was recruited and shipped to Gabon to work for a logging company. After three years Gabonese authorities deported him to Nigeria. He had never been paid.
Thirteen-year-old Tope came from neighbouring Benin on the promise of work, but when she arrived in Lagos found that work was in a brothel. When she became pregnant she was abandoned on the street.
"Children who work as domestic servants could be considered the most exploited children of all and the most difficult to protect," the report said.
"While some are sold into bondage by their parents or guardians and live in enforced isolation, others are enslaved without their consent or knowledge."
The report recommended that the military government tighten security at Nigeria's borders to prevent smuggling of children, as well as increasing spending on child welfare.
But saddled with a $32 billion foreign debt, the government has enough difficulties meeting even its current budget needs.
Human rights are not seen as being at the top of the agenda of a government condemned by Western countries for alleged rights abuses and insincerity in its plans to restore democracy.
"As a matter of urgency government should reappraise its scandalous complacency towards the rights of the child," the report said.
